claims.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys with pronounced lattice distortion or nanoscale features retain yield strength better at high temperature than conventional refractory alloys.
Refractory high-entropy alloys with pronounced lattice distortion or nanoscale features have altered high-temperature thermoelastic behavior relative to conventional refractory alloys.
Local lattice heterogeneities act as barriers to dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion caused by lattice heterogeneity limits thermally activated softening.
A single-phase refractory high-entropy alloy can be prepared with a uniform elemental and microstructural state.
The refractory high-entropy alloy and a lower-complexity conventional refractory alloy will be subjected to identical high-temperature tensile and thermal-expansion tests.
The proposed behavior is applicable around 800°C under constant-strain-rate, oxidation-free conditions.
The alloy contains intrinsic heterogeneous lattice distortions that locally modify stress fields.
The alloy may contain nanoscale clusters that locally modify stress fields.
Local lattice heterogeneities increase dislocation pinning and impede dislocation mobility.
Lattice heterogeneity can change dislocation configurations and slip behavior in refractory high-entropy alloys.
Dislocation pinning by lattice heterogeneities alters thermal-expansion behavior.
The refractory high-entropy alloy will show higher yield-strength retention during high-temperature deformation than the conventional refractory-alloy baseline.
The refractory high-entropy alloy will show a distinct high-temperature thermoelastic response relative to the conventional alloy.
The distinct thermoelastic response may be a plateau or a reduced thermal-expansion coefficient.
The conventional refractory-alloy baseline has lower lattice distortion and lacks the nanoscale features of the high-entropy alloy.
The comparison is applicable when the alloys have similar grain sizes and phase purities and oxidation is avoided.
Significant composition changes or substantially different strain rates may change the predicted behavior.

Failure to observe statistically greater strength retention or a distinct thermoelastic response, together with failure to observe enhanced pinning or lattice heterogeneity, would falsify the hypothesis.
